utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Would the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-95-5/18-R77.1, the Prosecutor versus Berko Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I am Judge O-Gon Kwon, Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber III, and have been designated to hear this initial appearance Professor Dr. Zecevic. First of all, I would like to make sure that Dr. Zecevic is following the proceedings in a language which he understand. Dr. Zecevic, are you receiving the interpretation into your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you turn on the -- press the microphone. Microphone. Turn on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Kwon, I receive normal audio feed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zecevic. It is my understanding that you are having back pain and spine-related conditions, so I don't mind you stand up from time to time whenever necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you kindly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like the counsel appearing for Dr. Zecevic to introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. On behalf of Dr. Zecevic, Guenael Mettraux, counsel, and Jesenka Residovic as legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. In light of some motions which we received from you this afternoon, Mr. Mettraux, I asked for the Prosecution to be represented at this hearing, although that would not normally be the case. So could the Prosecution please introduce yourself for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Alan Tieger, Fergal Gaynor, and Iain Reid appear for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Now Dr. Zecevic, while the Chamber has read your motions filed by your Defence counsel this afternoon, and we'll get to that shortly, I first have to go through certain formalities, so I'd like you to state your full name and date and place of your birth for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Berko Zecevic, university professor in Sarajevo, born on the 13th of December, 1949, in Srebrenica, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. It is my understanding that you were transferred to the United Nations Detention Unit in The Hague yesterday. Can I take it that your family is aware of that transfer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was able to speak with them on the phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would like to check that you have received a copy of the Order in Lieu of Indictment, dated 4th of February, 2011, in your own language, and that you have understood its content.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have received all material, and I have fully understood what is written there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you are represented here today by Mr. Mettraux. Are you satisfied with your representation here today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm more than satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable and be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed any further, I would like to deal with the motion which was filed confidentially by the Defence counsel, but before we go further, can I ask the reason why the motion was filed confidentially? If necessary, we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, Your Honour. I'm grateful for the question. We've indicated to the Prosecution we haven't received the record of these proceedings and weren't able to determine exactly which filings remain confidential and which were not. We'd be more than happy to file a public version of all three filings as soon as we are able to ascertain which of the filings remain confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then there's no problem. We discuss the matter in public session, including the motion for withdrawal of the Order in Lieu of Indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: There is none, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Dr. Zecevic, I understand from that motion that you are willing to testify in the Karadzic case. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never refused to testify in court. My reaction was prompted by the Prosecution and how they treated me, even though they were aware of my limitations. Given that I had spine surgery and that my ability to sit and to stand is extremely limited, I made a proposal to the Prosecution reflecting not my wishes but reflecting the result of my previous work with students, and so far I have been able to work with students for two or three lessons only, after which time I lose feeling in my toes on both feet. Following such lessons, I have to lie down for ten hours in order to regain feeling in my toes. It is certainly not appropriate for me to tell the Prosecution for how long I can testify, but I made a proposal to sit twice for 45 hours, but not longer than that, totaling 180. The Prosecution did not accept this proposal of mine, and this proposal was given completely honestly, without any bad intention on my part. I am somebody who has been co-operating with the OTP for the past 16 years. I provided hundreds and hundreds of hours of support to the OTP. I wrote hundreds of pages of various reports for them. Finally, I came to conclusion that any further co-operation with the OTP would result in me losing my integrity as a person, losing my freedom. Therefore, my actions were an attempt on my part to regain my integrity and to regain my freedom. Later on I became aware that they misinterpreted my requests and that it looked as though I did not want to help the court and that my actions were aimed against the court, which had never occurred to me. It had never occurred to me to bring into question the high esteem that I have for this court. Therefore, I'm prepared to testify. I would kindly ask you to take into account several basic facts when making your ruling as to the length of my testimony. I hope you will be able to take all elements into account. Today as we set out to come to this building, I travelled in a car for 20 minutes in very cramped conditions that are bad for my health. I was in the cell here. I was handcuffed both here and in Sarajevo, and I will be forced to wait for transport once my testimony begins as well. So if I were to testify for three to four hours each day, that means that there will be additional three to four hours of physical -- physically limiting circumstances that would be bad for my health. I have to tell you that as a professor who teaches, I have to be in good physical shape to be able to come to teach my students. I don't know that there are any cases where professors come on stretchers to teach and to work. By doing what I did, I undertook something that was aimed at ensuring the livelihood of my family. As a professor, as an active professor, I'm quite capable of giving very precise and prompt answers to any questions that are put to me. As an expert, I will provide answers to you, to the OTP, to the Defence. I have prepared various presentations that are quite illustrative in explaining the facts that are relevant to you, but please bear in mind that once I leave this Tribunal, I have to work in order to provide livelihood for my family and for myself and that I also need to be able to walk in order to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, but please let me understand correctly. While we are most certainly willing to accommodate your particular medical condition by tailoring our sitting sessions in a way that cause -- that causes you the least possible discomfort, but in a nutshell, it is not for you as a witness to dictate the terms of your testimony, including the total time of your evidence. So I have to ask you again whether it is your intention that you are willing to testify only for three hours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Kwon, I came here, and having consulted with my lawyer, I said that I would testify for as long as you consider that I need to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. I'm very pleased to hear of this development, and I will inform my colleagues in the Trial Chamber accordingly. Please be seated. Well, in light of this development, I would like first to hear from the Prosecution concerning the Defence motion for withdrawal of the Order in Lieu of Indictment. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We do not oppose the withdrawal of the contempt proceedings at the conclusion of the testimony of Dr. Zecevic. Now, I don't know if Mr. Zecevic's counsel is going to make any submissions concerning provisional release, but that's our principal position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will make submissions on provisional release once this matter has been dealt with by the Chamber. We're having difficulties, as indicated to the Office of the Prosecutor, obtaining the necessary visas that would permit Mr. Zecevic -- Dr. Zecevic, to stay on Dutch territory. We understand from the Registry's indications that the change of status on the part of Mr. Zecevic from an accused to a witness would greatly facilitate matters and that they stand ready at this moment to contact the Dutch authority to facilitate his stay were he to be released from the UNDU today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. I don't think your filing of provisional release will be necessary. I have discussed this matter with my colleagues in the Trial Chamber already, and we consider it prudent to simply suspend the Order in Lieu of Indictment, as well as the order for detention on remand until Professor Zecevic's testimony in the Karadzic case is completed. We will issue a written decision to this effect after -- after this hearing, as soon as practicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We're very grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then on a practical matter, I take it that, Mr. Tieger or Mr. Gaynor, we can hear the testimony of Professor Dr. Zecevic when the Karadzic proceedings resume on Tuesday next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We can start with Dr. Zecevic, or we can continue with the witness who is currently in the middle of his evidence. We're prepared to go as Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me consult the Legal Officer of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Considering the circumstances, it is better to hear Mr. Zecevic as soon as possible, but the question is whether the witness we are currently hearing can be released until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, he can be released. He's -- I think he's currently in The Hague now. He has elderly relatives who he cares for, so he would be keen for him to return home as soon as possible. If I can say this: There are two hours of cross-examination ordered for him, examination-in-chief is almost complete. So if we were to deal with him first thing on Tuesday, perhaps we could -- we could send him home on Tuesday morning and then start with Dr. Zecevic. That might be the better option possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation on this, Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply to indicate that the representatives of Dr. Karadzic have informed us that they would be willing and ready to start with Dr. Zecevic on Tuesday. They had to make certain arrangements for the expert to come here. This is the only additional information we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To make it simple, why don't we start with Mr. Zecevic, Mr. Gaynor, on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Mettraux, we have also received your request to be present in the courtroom during Dr. Zecevic's testimony, and I understand that neither the Prosecution nor Mr. Karadzic's team opposes that request. I'm not in a position right now to give our decision on that motion, but you will have it on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any matters to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Not from this side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Nothing from us either. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: at 3.24 p.m.
